h1: Beer with Ethiopian injera and berbere spiced stews
title: Beer with Ethiopian Injera and Stews | Craft Beer School
desc: How to pair beer with Ethiopian food: injera, doro wat, misir wot and kitfo. Which styles suit the sourness and the spice. Also why they work.
teaser: Injera is sour, berbere is warm and the plate is shared. Here is what to pour with it.
standfirst: Ethiopian food is built on a spongy, slightly sour flatbread and rich stews seasoned with berbere. Beer handles both well if you pick the right style. Here is how.
sections:
A traditional Ethiopian meal arrives on a large round tray covered with injera, a soft, spongy flatbread made from teff flour. The batter is fermented for a few days, which gives injera a gentle sour tang. Stews and sides are spooned on top. Everyone tears off pieces of injera to scoop them up with their right hand.

The stews are called wot or wat. Doro wat is a chicken stew simmered with a lot of onion and a deep red spice paste. Misir wot is red lentils cooked the same way. Gomen is greens. Kitfo is minced beef seasoned with spiced butter and chilli, served raw or lightly cooked. Many dishes are vegetarian, which makes the cuisine easy for many Indian readers.

Berbere is the spice blend behind many of the stews. It is built on dried chilli with garlic, ginger, fenugreek, coriander and other warm spices. The heat is rounded and aromatic rather than sharp. Because the sauces also carry a lot of onion cooked down slowly, there is sweetness underneath the spice.

That mix of chilli heat, savoury depth and sourness from the injera is a useful test for beer. Heat sticks to the tongue and builds. Strong alcohol and heavy bitterness make it feel hotter. Carbonation, sweetness and low bitterness calm it.

• Wheat beer or witbier. Soft and fizzy. A witbier is also lightly spiced with coriander and orange peel. It matches the aromatic spice and refreshes between bites.
  • Saison. Dry, peppery and highly carbonated. The spicy yeast character meets the berbere. The dryness lifts the richness of the stews.
  • Amber lager or Vienna lager. Gentle toasty malt gives a little sweetness against the heat and does not fight the sour injera.
  • Pale ale with moderate bitterness. A citrusy but not aggressive example works with the chicken stew. A very hoppy IPA tends to turn bitter against chilli.
  • Light, crisp lager. Not exciting, but it is a safe choice for a long meal with lots of dishes.

These are suggestions, not rules. Your own palate and the heat of the dish decide.

Very high alcohol beers can sharpen the heat of the berbere. Heavily roasted stouts and big imperial beers will overwhelm the more delicate lentil and greens dishes. Strongly hopped IPAs add bitterness to chilli heat and the two compound each other.

Sour beers are tempting because injera is sour, but stacking acid on acid can make the meal feel sharp. If you try one, pick a gentle example and take small sips.
A tasting set-up for a group

Ethiopian food is made for sharing, so a pairing evening works well as a group. Set up a few beers before the food arrives. Pour small measures of around 60 ml each. Let people taste with each dish in turn. Our guide to setting up a beer tasting has a simple format to follow. The glassware guide explains why a tulip or a stemmed glass helps with aromatic styles.

Keep drinking sensible. Offer water at every seat and have good non-alcoholic options on the table. Pace the beers over the whole meal. Nobody should drive afterwards.

Cold dulls a beer's aroma and warmth lifts it. Serve lagers cold, around 4 to 6 °C. Serve wheat beers and saisons slightly warmer, around 6 to 8 °C, so the yeast spice comes through. Our note on serving temperature gives the basics.

Taste between mouthfuls rather than during one. Eat a bite of injera, then a sip of beer, then notice what the beer does to the heat and the sourness. That sequence is the whole technique.

Teff flour is not common in India. Ethiopian restaurants exist in a few big cities. Some stores stock teff and berbere. If you cook at home, authentic injera needs teff and a few days of fermenting. A pancake of rice flour and sorghum is not the same, but it gives you something to taste against.

Whatever you cook or order, write notes. Name the sweetness, the sourness, the heat and the aroma, then say what the beer changed. That habit separates a pleasant dinner from real tasting practice.
faqs: What beer goes with Ethiopian food?
Wheat beer, saison, amber lager and a moderately bitter pale ale all work. They handle the spice and the sour injera without adding too much bitterness.
Should I avoid IPA with berbere?
A very hoppy IPA often tastes more bitter against chilli heat. A softer pale ale is safer. Try a small pour first.
Does sour beer match sour injera?
It can, but acid on acid can feel sharp. If you try it, choose a gentle sour beer and take small sips.
Many stews carry real chilli heat from berbere, though it is rounded and aromatic. Some dishes, such as lentils with mild spice, are gentler.
